summary: PeptAI's programme overview describes a computational peptide/protein design effort targeting taste receptors (TAS1R2/TAS1R3 for sweet, TAS2R family for bitter) for food, beverage, and nutrition applications. The programme is explicitly described as early-stage, with receptor modelling and design as the current activity, prior to any laboratory measurement. No experimental results are reported; candidates remain hypotheses until cell-based assay data are generated.

content_blocks.title: Programme Overview – Target at a Glance
content_blocks.content: Targets: TAS1R2/TAS1R3 (sweet receptor heterodimer, class C GPCR) and TAS2R family (~25 receptors, class A GPCR, bitter). Modality: designed peptide and protein modulators. Expression: taste cells of tongue and palate, plus extra-oral tissues. Applications: food, beverage and nutrition. Pathway: taste compound → TAS1R or TAS2R receptor → G protein signalling → taste cell response → perceived taste.

content_blocks.title: Biology
content_blocks.content: Sweet taste detected by TAS1R2/TAS1R3 heterodimer (Nelson et al. 2001, Cell). Bitter taste detected by TAS2R family (Chandrashekar et al. 2000, Cell) with overlapping specificities across ~25 receptors (Meyerhof et al. 2009, Chem Senses). Both receptor types signal through G proteins in taste cells. Ligands bind at multiple sites including large extracellular domains on the sweet receptor, providing multiple design entry points.

content_blocks.title: Validation
content_blocks.content: Receptors and their roles in taste are well established; receptor-based assays are widely used in flavour research. Sweet receptor has a long record as a screening target for sweeteners and enhancers. Open question: whether designed peptides and proteins can modulate these receptors with the selectivity and stability required for a food ingredient. No proprietary experimental validation data are reported.

content_blocks.title: Landscape and Gap
content_blocks.content: Sugar reduction and bitter masking are central problems in food/beverage development. Current solutions (small molecules, extracts, blends) have limitations: aftertaste, stability, regulatory burden. Designed peptides and proteins offer tunable receptor engagement and potentially cleaner taste profiles; protein ingredients have a clear route into food applications.

content_blocks.title: Design Challenges and Risks
content_blocks.content: 1. Receptor assembly: sweet receptor heterodimer is harder to model and assay than a single chain. 2. Bitter breadth: each bitter receptor recognises many compounds, making selectivity difficult to define. 3. Sensory translation: cell assays only partly predict perception; sensory panels are the final test. 4. Regulatory path: new food ingredients require safety evaluation, shaping the choice of design format.

content_blocks.title: Decision Criteria (How We Will Know)
content_blocks.content: A candidate advances only on measured receptor activity in a cell-based assay, followed by sensory evaluation. Predicted binding alone does not advance a candidate. This confirms no candidates have yet passed the experimental gate.

content_blocks.title: Stage and Next Steps
content_blocks.content: The programme is explicitly described as early. Current activity: receptor modelling and design. Next step: receptor-activity assays. No experimental data have been generated yet; all designs are currently hypotheses.

content_blocks.title: PeptAI Platform Description
content_blocks.content: PeptAI designs peptides and proteins against defined molecular targets. Each design passes through staged computational filters for structure, binding geometry and developability. Laboratory measurement is the only gate that makes a candidate real. Measured sequence-activity pairs are retained to improve models. This describes a computational-first, iterative design-test cycle.

key_findings: Programme is explicitly early-stage (TRL 1–2): receptor modelling and computational design are underway, but no laboratory measurements have been reported.

Targets are TAS1R2/TAS1R3 (sweet, class C GPCR heterodimer) and TAS2R family (~25 receptors, class A GPCR, bitter); both are well-validated in the literature but not yet validated by PeptAI's own experiments.
Modality is designed peptides and proteins; application domain is food, beverage and nutrition (not pharmaceutical).
Advancement gate requires measured receptor activity in a cell-based assay followed by sensory evaluation — predicted binding alone is insufficient; no candidates have yet cleared this gate.

Key risks: heterodimer complexity for sweet receptor modelling/assay, selectivity challenges across 25 bitter receptors, imperfect translation from cell assays to sensory perception, and food ingredient regulatory requirements.
Platform uses staged computational filters (structure, binding geometry, developability) with iterative learning from measured sequence-activity pairs.
No quantitative experimental data (IC50, EC50, % modulation, etc.) are reported anywhere in the document.
